segments.t: Magüi explains how she has known Paquita since childhood in Getafe, and actress Lidia San José recalls her start in television commercials. When event organiser Piti phones about tonight's Cosmopolitan party, Paquita quickly sends Lidia in Maca's place. Listen to the conversation first.
Llevo toda la vida con Paquita, desde los cinco años.
Mi madre le cortaba el pelo cuando tenía la agencia en Getafe.
Es una de las pocas personas que puede llamarme Paca.
Lo primero que hice fue un anuncio de publicidad.
Todas empezamos haciendo publi.
Espera, que le voy a preguntar a Paquita.
Paquita, es Piti. No tiene confirmación de Maca para Cosmopolitan.
Es que no llegó ningún mail.
A mí no me ha llegado invitación para los Cosmo.
Dile a Piti que me invite.
Cariño, esta noche Maca no puede, tiene lo de la Seminci.
Pero te mando a Lidia San José.
¿Cóctel o largo? Cóctel.
Venga. ¿Tienes look?
Let's go through the scene line by line.
Llevo toda la vida con Paquita, desde los cinco años.

'I've spent my whole life with Paquita, since I was five.' Once again that handy duration word appears, literally I carry all the life with Paquita. For age, Spanish says from the five years rather than since I was five.
Mi madre le cortaba el pelo cuando tenía la agencia en Getafe.

'My mother used to cut her hair when she had the agency in Getafe.' Instead, of saying her hair, Spanish says cut to her the hair, putting a tiny word for to her before cut. Both past forms end in a smooth ongoing sound for habits back then.
Es una de las pocas personas que puede llamarme Paca.

'She's one of the few people who can call me Paca.' Paca is the traditional nickname for Francisca, while Paquita adds a warm diminutive ending. Notice how me tacks straight onto the end of to call as one combined word.
Lo primero que hice fue un anuncio de publicidad.

'The first thing I did was a commercial.' Spanish has a neat neuter word at the start that turns first into the first thing without needing a separate word for thing. The final pair literally means an announcement of advertising.
Todas empezamos haciendo publi.

'We all started out doing commercials.' Paquita uses the feminine plural for all because she means all the women in the room. At the end, she clips the word for advertising down to its casual two-syllable showbiz short form.
Espera, que le voy a preguntar a Paquita.

'Hold on, I'm going to ask Paquita.' The opening is the casual command form of wait. Then going to plus to ask works just like English going to ask, with a little word for her pointing ahead to Paquita.
Paquita, es Piti. No tiene confirmación de Maca para Cosmopolitan.

'Paquita, it's Piti. She doesn't have Maca's confirmation for Cosmopolitan.' Instead, of adding an apostrophe-s to Maca, Spanish flips the order to confirmation of Maca. The word for introduces the event she was meant to attend.
Es que no llegó ningún mail.

'The thing is, no email arrived.' Starting a sentence with literally it is that is Spain's favourite everyday way to offer an excuse or explanation. Because no sits before arrived, the word for any after it reinforces the negative rather than cancelling it.
A mí no me ha llegado invitación para los Cosmo.

'I haven't received an invitation to the Cosmos.' Literally, to me has not arrived invitation, which is how Spanish naturally talks about post or messages reaching you. Cosmo is short for the Cosmopolitan awards party.
Dile a Piti que me invite.
'Tell Piti to invite me.' The first word packs tell and to her together into two syllables. Where English uses an infinitive in tell her to invite me, Spanish says tell her that she invite me.
Cariño, esta noche Maca no puede, tiene lo de la Seminci.

'Darling, Maca can't make it tonight, she has the Seminci festival.' This affectionate opener literally means fondness or love, and Paquita uses it with almost everyone. Near the end, a tiny neuter phrase means that Seminci business.
Pero te mando a Lidia San José.

'But I'm sending you Lidia San José.' Present-tense I send you covers something Paquita is arranging right this moment. The little personal marker appears again before Lidia San José because she is a person.
¿Cóctel o largo? Cóctel.
'Cocktail or full-length? Cocktail.' Checking the dress code takes just three words, leaving out the word for dress altogether. The word for long stands on its own to mean a full-length evening gown.
Venga. ¿Tienes look?

'Alright. Do you have an outfit?' That brisk first word literally means come, and Spaniards say it constantly for alright, come on, or deal. Spanish also borrows the English word look for a styled party outfit. Now let's listen to the whole scene again.
Llevo toda la vida con Paquita, desde los cinco años.
Mi madre le cortaba el pelo cuando tenía la agencia en Getafe.
Es una de las pocas personas que puede llamarme Paca.
Lo primero que hice fue un anuncio de publicidad.
Todas empezamos haciendo publi.
Espera, que le voy a preguntar a Paquita.
Paquita, es Piti. No tiene confirmación de Maca para Cosmopolitan.
Es que no llegó ningún mail.
A mí no me ha llegado invitación para los Cosmo.
Dile a Piti que me invite.
Cariño, esta noche Maca no puede, tiene lo de la Seminci.
Pero te mando a Lidia San José.
¿Cóctel o largo? Cóctel.
Venga. ¿Tienes look?
You heard how Spanish talks about doing something since childhood, how emails 'arrive' rather than 'get received', and how Paquita improvises an invitation on the phone. See you in the next scene.
¡Hasta luego!
